title: Clamp Meters and Load Measurement

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Electrical room with an open lighting panel, dead-front on; qualified lead and a tech in arc-rated PPE; true-RMS clamp meter in hand. Medium shot of Matthew outside the approach boundary.
scenes.on_screen: Job Mindset: clamping in a panel is energized work | PPE per the label | hands behind the tactile barrier
scenes.says: Load measurement at a lighting panel. Even though you never open the circuit, clamping a conductor in a panel is energized work. The hazards are shock and arc flash. So: PPE per the equipment label, qualified supervision, hands behind the clamp's tactile barrier. Before you go, plan which circuits you need, bring a true-RMS clamp, and know where you'll measure if you can't reach a single conductor.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Close-up of a clamp meter's jaws, dial and the tactile barrier.
scenes.on_screen: Clamp meter: senses the magnetic field | no need to open the circuit | AC clamp vs AC/DC (Hall effect)
scenes.says: A clamp meter measures current by sensing the magnetic field around a conductor. You don't open the circuit or put the meter in series, which is a big safety and time advantage over a DMM's amps jack. AC clamps measure AC only. AC/DC clamps use a Hall-effect sensor and also read DC. Most also do volts, ohms and continuity through leads, with the same CAT rating rules.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tech clamps a single lighting branch-circuit hot conductor, centered in the jaw; reading on screen. Presenter voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Clamp ONE conductor | center it | close the jaws fully | true-RMS on LED loads
scenes.says: The golden rule: clamp one conductor at a time. Here, one lighting branch-circuit hot, centered in the jaw, jaws fully closed. That's the load current on that circuit. Use a true-RMS clamp, because LED drivers and electronic ballasts draw distorted current, and an average-responding clamp can read significantly low. Zero DC clamps first, and record the reading with the circuit number and time.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tech clamps hot and neutral together; reading drops to near zero.
scenes.on_screen: Hot + neutral together = near zero | significant reading = current returning another way
scenes.says: Now hot and neutral together. Near zero. Equal and opposite currents cancel. That's useful: if you clamp hot and neutral together and get a significant reading, some current's coming back another way. A ground fault, a neutral tied to another circuit, or a neutral-to-ground connection downstream. A dedicated leakage clamp reads milliamps accurately; a standard clamp may not.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Tech clamps the panel neutral; then phase readings shown side by side.
scenes.on_screen: 80% threshold: 15 A = 12 | 20 A = 16 | 30 A = 24 | neutral higher than any phase = report it
scenes.says: Now the panel neutral. Compare circuit loads to 80 percent of the breaker: 12 amps on a 15, 16 on a 20, 24 on a 30. A circuit regularly over that should be reported. Check phase balance too. A neutral current higher than any phase current, on a panel with lots of electronic loads, can mean harmonic loading. Report it.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen: Can't reach a single conductor? Measure elsewhere or get a qualified lead | never pull slack in panel conductors
scenes.says: Don't force the jaws between tightly packed conductors. If you can't reach a single conductor without disturbing others, measure somewhere else, like at the fixture junction box after de-energizing and installing a test loop, or get help from a qualified lead. For small currents, some techs loop a short test whip through the jaw and divide by the turns. Never pull slack in energized panel conductors.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Fixture junction box with a clamp on the supply conductor in inrush mode; bank of LED fixtures switched on; peak reading captured.
scenes.on_screen: Inrush: breakers trip at switch-on | welded contacts | sensors failing early -> capture it for your lead
scenes.says: At the fixture junction box, inrush mode. LED drivers draw a very brief, very high current at switch-on, often many times running current for a fraction of a millisecond. Switch the bank on, and the meter captures the peak. Use it when breakers trip at switch-on but not after, contacts weld, or sensors fail early. At LT2, recognize the symptom and capture the data for your lead.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew in the electrical room, medium shot.
scenes.on_screen: Dark + drawing current = internal problem | zero current + good voltage = open input
scenes.says: One more fast check: a dark fixture drawing near-normal current points to the lamp, LED board or driver output. Zero current with correct input voltage points to an open input. One conductor, true-RMS, PPE in the panel. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Filmed with proper PPE at a lighting panel under supervision, per the lesson's video suggestion: single conductor, hot and neutral together, panel neutral, then inrush at a fixture junction box as a bank of LED fixtures switches on. Keep the presenter outside approach boundaries. Mask meter brands.
